sweep_summary: One stress-titled item for nort2723: Ding 2001 (LTBA 24.2), the pitch accent analysis of Niuwozi Prinmi. It was already held by the project as a text-less scan with only pp.1-4 scanned; this search of works with stress in the title scanned the remaining 23 pages (tesseract, 300 dpi, sequential) and read the whole paper. It is a first-hand lexical-tone description: no word stress (p.59 'the line between tone and stress is clear-cut'; no other mention), a single marked H whose locus (positions 1-4 of a <=4-syllable domain) and one-syllable rightward spread carry the contrast (Table 7 p.72, pp.73-74), which Ding calls a pitch accent system (a subtype of tone in his typology, p.62). It refines rather than changes the catalog's 'tonal' coding: it is the source of the 'pitch accent' half of the record's tonal-OR-pitch accent flag, which Daudey 2014 fn.97 (the deciding source, held) and Hyman 2009 (held) answer. Variety caveat: Niuwozi is Central Prinmi per Ding 2012/2014 (Daudey pp.3-4) and Southern per Lu 1983 (Ding p.57); Glottolog's assignment to nort2723 is computerized, so it is a sister variety of the catalog's Wadu Pumi. Daudey 2014 remains the best deciding source; nothing was found that supersedes it. Glottolog reference page 112700 was downloaded and confirms the bibliographic record (no DOI/URL; SALA id ding2001pitch).

new_statements.reading: Niuwozi Prinmi has no word stress; its word prosody is a culminative lexical tone system in which one marked H is lexically placed on syllable 1, 2, 3 or 4 of a prosodic domain (max four syllables) and may spread one syllable rightwards, remaining syllables default L; Ding labels this 'pitch accent' as a subtype of tone (not stress). This matches the catalog's 'tonal' (culminative word-tone) coding and is the origin of the 'pitch accent' alternative in the tonal-OR-pitch accent flag; it is on a sister (Central, per Ding 2012/2014) variety rather than Wadu Pumi itself.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (culminative word-tone, no word-stress rule) rests on the best and only description of Wadu Pumi, Daudey's 2014 626-page PhD grammar with a dedicated tone chapter, which we hold; every quoted segment was found verbatim at the cited pages (pp.10-11, 64, 65 and fn.97). The grammar nowhere posits word stress (one hedged aside on alternating verbs, p.~72). Independent open sources downloaded now for sister Northern/Central Prinmi varieties (Jacques 2011; Ding 2001; Hyman 2009's reanalysis of Ding, which states there is no reason to think the toned syllable is stressed) all describe a one-tone-per-domain system with rightward H spread and no stress, so the 'pitch accent' label in older Ding work is a terminological alternative, not a contradiction; Daudey addresses it explicitly. sources.note: First-hand description of Niuwozi Prinmi (Ninglang County, Yunnan; Ding's own field data). No word stress is posited anywhere: p.59 'the line between tone and stress is clear-cut', and 'stress' occurs nowhere else in the paper (a full-text search for stress/accent the full scanned). Monosyllables contrast falling / high / rising (p.63, ex.3); in polysyllables the only contrast is WHERE the single marked H sits in a prosodic domain of up to four syllables (positions 1-4) plus whether it spreads one syllable rightwards, all other syllables surfacing L (Table 7 p.72; pp.73-74); the author's defi…

sources.quote: Northern Pumi (Shuiluo, Mudiqing): 'Pumi dialects have tonal contrasts'; monosyllables H/F/R analysed as H, HL, LH; in polysyllables far fewer than 3^n patterns, generated by 'the place of the high tone in the prosodic domain, and whether this high tone can spread'; the H 'spreads rightwards, so that syllables situated on its left are realized with a low tone'. Fn.3: 'Since the category of Pitch Accent is difficult to define rigorously cross-linguistically (Hyman 2009), we will avoid this term'. No word stress is described.
sources.note: Independent tonal description of two other Northern Pumi varieties (Shuiluo, Mudiqing) confirming H-placement-plus-rightward-spread tone with no stress; now obtained (downloaded preprint).

sources.quote: Reanalysis of Ding's (2001) Prinmi as /H/, /HL/, /LH/ with one toned syllable per word and default L elsewhere: 'one syllable per word is marked for one of three underlying tones ... (Other than carrying a tonal specification, there is no reason to think that the toned syllable is stressed.)' Supports coding the system as (culminative) tone rather than stress/accent.
